newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cabinet adopts plan for firms' sell-offs.
newsitem.headline: Polish cabinet adopts plan for firms' sell-offs.

text.p: The Polish cabinet on Monday adopted a privatisation plan that opens some sensitive sectors for sale in 1997 and provides for the sale of most state assets by the end of century, a government official said.
"A large part of assets still state-owned will be privatised within the next four years," deputy Privatisation Minister Andrzej Zebrowski told a news briefing.

Under the programme, called "The privatisation outline for 1997", but applying also to the next four years, about 115 large and medium-size state-owned firms would be sold to strategic investors in 1997 and five placed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange, according to a government press office statement.
Up to 300 small companies would be sold directly through simplified procedures over the period, the statement said.
The programme provides for opening new industries for privatisation in 1997, including energy, telecommunications, chemicals, oil and distillery.
The government earlier said next year's large privatisation projects would include the partial sale of the KGHM copper combine, refineries and national air carrier LOT.
The privatisation of the telecommunications monopolist TPSA is due to start next year.
It also said it planned to privatise about 10 large power stations by 2000 after launching a programme to bring competition to the energy sector next year.

Zebrowski, whose ministry was due to be replaced on Tuesday by a more powerful treasury portfolio, said that, from the next year on, privatisation would be linked to several government programmes, which envisage the creation of investment funds.

Under the most important of such schemes, new pension funds would be set up as part of a government plan to reform the inefficient social security system and endowed with shares of firms undergoing privatisation as start-up capital.

Other funds with shares of privatised companies would be created under two compensation schemes -- for former owners whose property was confiscated after the World War Two by the then communist authorities and for pensioners and public workers for overdue salary rises in early 1990s.
About 400 state-owned companies with good financial results would be earmarked for contributing some of their shares to the funds.
Zebrowski added that the government would speed up the implementation of a programme that allows Poland's commercial creditors to swap debt for equity in companies undergoing privatisation.
